author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: A Place for the Departing
subtitle: The Lanternweald — expansion pass two
content:
The first person to ask whether they were allowed to leave the Lanternweald without saying goodbye was standing in my kitchen.

They were holding a loaf of bread in both hands. Mara had baked it that morning, and the crust had split along the top like a small mountain range. The traveler had bought it with two copper buttons and an offer to mend the bakery curtains.

"I can give the bread back," they said.

"Why?"

"If it makes things easier."

I stared at them. They stared at the floor.

It was the third time they had come to see me that week, and the first time they'd been able to ask the question.

"You can leave," I said. "You don't owe anyone a reason."

The traveler's shoulders loosened. Not all the way.

"What about the register?"

"Neri's arrival book?"

They nodded.

"It's not supposed to be a leash."

"Everyone knows when I come in. Pip reads out the visitor names sometimes. I don't want anyone knowing which road I'm taking."

I had assumed that a place full of doors would make leaving simple. I'd assumed many things since arriving here. My notebook was becoming a monument to the hazards of assuming.

"Can you wait until I check how the departure book works?" I asked.

They hesitated.

"You don't have to wait," I corrected. "I can meet you at the door later, if you want help. Or you can go now."

"Later," they said. "And please don't tell the man with the hook."

Maui chose that precise moment to come through the window.

Not the door. The window.

He had a string of damp rope over one shoulder and sand in his hair. One foot landed on the kitchen stool. The stool protested so loudly that the traveler flinched.

"Good news!" Maui announced. "I secured the—"

"Window," I said.

"Very efficient route."

"Door."

"Slower route."

The traveler went white.

I set the bread on the table and stepped between them and the window.

"Maui, I need you outside for a minute."

He looked at my face and lost the grin.

"Of course."

That was progress. Last month he would have asked five questions and answered three of them himself.

After he climbed back out, I walked the traveler to the covered passage behind the bakery. They gave me the name they'd chosen for the arrival book: Lark. They said it softly, like a name they weren't certain they were permitted to keep.

We agreed on a meeting place near the eastern arch at dusk. They did not tell me why they were leaving, and I did not ask.

When I returned, Maui was standing outside with the injured expression of a man denied the chance to make a heroic speech.

"Did I scare someone?"

"Yes."

"I didn't know they were there."

"I know."

He folded his arms. "If someone needs to leave, I can escort them. I know every safe path from the cove."

"They explicitly asked me not to tell you."

His expression sharpened.

"Do they think I would hurt them?"

"I don't know."

"Then why—"

"Because that's their choice."

He looked toward the bakery. A child was chasing a dropped apple across the square. The world went on around his silence.

"You think I can't be trusted," he said.

"I think you want to be useful. That's not the same thing as being invited."

Maui turned away.

I let him have the space.

By afternoon I had a list of problems. Some were obvious: Pip sometimes announced arrival names before asking permission. The arrival book had a column labeled EXPECTED RETURN, as though every departure were a promise. Neri kept a spare key for every door but hadn't written down who could request one. The eastern arch had a railing that blocked one side of the approach.

The least obvious problem was that everyone wanted to help in their own preferred way. Which meant that a traveler who needed privacy had to reject kindness five times before getting what they'd asked for.

Neri listened while I explained.

They rested both hands over their walking stick.

"The register was meant to protect travelers. If someone went missing, we wanted to know which way to search."

"Search only if they've asked to be searched for," I said.

Neri's eyes dimmed. "That is a difficult thing to say after you've lost someone."

"I know."

"Do you?"

I thought of the door to my old life. All the people I couldn't name, some of whom might be looking for me. I thought of how sick I felt when someone assumed not remembering meant I belonged to whoever recognized me first.

"Yes," I said. "More than I'd like."

Neri looked toward the arches.

"We used to close them in storms."

"Did the traveler agree?"

They did not answer.

The silence bothered me enough to write it down.

At dusk I met Lark beside the eastern arch. The air smelled of wet stone and burned rosemary. They had one travel pack and the loaf of bread wrapped in cloth.

"Are you coming with me?" they asked.

"Only as far as you want."

"Can you stand back while I open it?"

"Of course."

I went to the railing and stood facing the square. Behind me a brass latch clicked. Cold air touched my neck.

"Jasper?"

I turned.

Lark was waiting in the doorway, their shoulders straight now.

"Thank you for not asking."

"Safe travels."

They smiled once and stepped through. The door closed.

Nothing terrible happened. No bell rang in protest. The lights at the well stayed lit.

I found Maui at the cove checking the new tide chart. He had covered the little crab drawing with a square of parchment, then uncovered it again, as if even the crab's expression needed approval.

"They left," I said.

"I know."

"How?"

"I saw the door light change." He paused. "I stayed here."

I leaned against the railing beside him.

"Was it hard?"

"Yes."

I appreciated the answer.

He stared at the horizon. "I've spent so much of my life proving I can get someone home. I never considered that getting out of the way might be the useful thing."

I found his hand where it rested on the rail. He turned his palm up.

"I didn't tell you because Lark asked me not to," I said. "Not because I don't trust you. Sometimes someone's privacy belongs to them even when keeping it makes us uncomfortable."

"I know that now." He glanced sideways. "I might forget it."

"Then I'll remind you."

"You're very good at being annoying."

"I've been practicing."

He lifted my hand and kissed my knuckles. The gesture was so unexpected that warmth climbed up my neck.

"May I?" he asked, close enough that his voice lowered.

"You may."

He kissed me gently beside the new tide sign. The sea moved beneath us. He did not promise to be perfect, and I did not need him to.

The following morning, Pip and I rewrote the arrival register. There would be an optional contact and a private note indicating whether someone wanted assistance leaving. Nobody would read names aloud without permission. And where the old page said EXPECTED RETURN, we wrote one question instead:

DO YOU WANT SOMEONE TO WAIT FOR YOU?

Lark's row remained blank.

For the first time, I understood that a blank line could be an act of care.
